answer.text: Two research traditions address human interaction differently: network physicalization turns relational or graph data into tangible, manipulable objects, while haptic feedback in AR and VR uses actuators to render the sensation of touching a virtual object that remains purely digital.

The core distinguishing difference is where the interaction lives: physicalization keeps a persistent physical artifact a person can pick up without any headset or glove, whereas haptic feedback simulates touch on demand and requires hardware worn on the body to close the loop between vision and touch.

In the tangible IP network simulation built by Kobayashi, Hirano, Narita and Ishii, users create nodes and modify parameters by placing physical tokens on a table, producing an explorable network model with no digital display of the network itself.

Comparable tangible-token systems, including Urp for urban wind and light and a Micro Smart Grid explainer on an interactive tabletop, show that mapping relationships onto movable tokens is a recurring design pattern for network data, letting learners discover structure through practical exploration and supporting simultaneous multi-user interaction around a shared table.

Data physicalization research argues physical formats can broaden participation, support analytics, and promote creative expression in ways screens cannot, and that physicalizing sensor and AI data can make it accessible to non-expert audiences.

Low-cost 3D printing and laser cutting make physicalization more resourceful for researchers, since digital-physical toolkits let designers rapidly prototype tangible network models from inexpensive, reusable materials rather than custom electronics.

Physicalization remains a comparatively niche, early-stage research area, described by visualization researchers and interdisciplinary seminar participants as historically marginal, with open conceptual, technical, and empirical questions unresolved.

Because physical tokens are, in Ishii and Ullmer's phrase, relatively inflexible compared with digital bits, a fabricated network model is hard to reconfigure for a new dataset, and the Micro Smart Grid team found even adding reflective plastic to tokens created new material trade-offs and required constant readjustment under changing light and heat.

Fabrication itself creates accessibility barriers, since small, low-cost actuators for shape-changing displays remain limited in resolution and availability, and toolkit studies found lay designers struggling with assembly instructions, material choice, and precise alignment.

Haptic feedback in AR and VR benefits from a well-funded, rapidly growing industry, with the global haptic technology market valued at 8.08 billion US dollars in 2022 and a projected 6.2 percent annual growth rate spanning electronics, automotive, gaming, and healthcare.

Large industrial labs such as Meta's Reality Labs Research have invested years of multidisciplinary work in soft robotics, microfluidics, hand tracking, and perceptual science to make haptic gloves feel believable.

Haptic feedback generalizes across many use cases without a bespoke physical build for every dataset, since wearable devices have been validated for exploring texture, stiffness, size, shape, temperature, weight, and orientation, tele-haptics extend the same sensors to remote human interaction, and haptic alerts support braille-like displays and tactile notifications for users with visual or hearing impairments.

Haptic hardware remains expensive: consumer haptic vests cost between 499 and 1000 US dollars and weigh 1.5 to 2.5 kilograms with poor game integration, while historic instrumented gloves cost 8,800 US dollars and top-end head-mounted displays reached 50,000 US dollars.

High-fidelity research-grade devices such as the sigma.x, omega.x, delta.x, and Phantom Premium series remain costly with a limited workspace, and most existing high-fidelity rendering devices are still relatively costly for typical labs.

Technical complexity is a persistent barrier, since actuators generate too much heat and are too large, rigid, and power-hungry for comfortable all-day wear, forcing researchers into unproven soft-robotics and microfluidic materials built almost from scratch, and even state-of-the-art gloves cannot stop a user's fingers from closing through a virtual object.

The haptic technology market analysis flags high production costs, a lack of standardized content formats, and integration challenges across hardware, software, and platforms as ongoing obstacles to affordability.

Network physicalization literature clusters around tangible tabletop systems such as Urp and the IP network simulator, qualitative case studies of data sculptures classified by a semiotic taxonomy, and toolkit studies of lay fabrication behavior such as tinkering and iterative refinement, while haptic-feedback literature clusters around industrial glove-development case studies, wearable-device reviews mapping tested devices against object properties, market analyses, and technical surveys detailing specifications such as a glove's 133 tactile points per hand or another's 11 degrees of freedom.

On well-researched history, network physicalization scores roughly 2 out of 5, repeatedly described as a historically niche corner of visualization research with unresolved foundations, while haptic feedback scores roughly 4 out of 5, given decades of commercial hardware history and a now multi-billion-dollar, tracked industry.

On resourcefulness, network physicalization scores about 3 out of 5 since accessible fabrication tools expand what researchers can build though actuator options remain limited, while haptic feedback scores about 4 out of 5, drawing on soft robotics, microfluidics, dielectric elastomers, tele-haptics, and a broad commercial device ecosystem.

On practicality, network physicalization scores about 3 out of 5, performing well in fixed exhibits and education but suffering from the physical inflexibility of built tokens once a dataset changes, while haptic feedback scores about 2 out of 5, since comfort, heat, weight, and incomplete physical realism still limit everyday use even in flagship prototypes.

On accessibility for researchers, network physicalization scores about 4 out of 5, since low-cost, hobbyist-accessible fabrication materials let researchers prototype tangible network models relatively quickly, while haptic feedback scores about 2 out of 5, since believable tactile rendering requires expertise across soft robotics, microfluidics, and perceptual science plus costly custom manufacturing.

On accessibility for common users, network physicalization scores about 3 out of 5, since finished tangible exhibits are intuitive and headset-free but typically bespoke, one-off installations, while haptic feedback scores about 2 out of 5, since consumer suits and gloves costing hundreds to over a thousand US dollars, combined with weight and integration problems, still limit mainstream adoption.

Taken together, network physicalization offers an accessible entry point for embodied, multi-user network interaction but rests on a thinner research history and rigid, dataset-specific artifacts, while haptic feedback sits on a deeper, better-funded research base with broader applicability, though its practical maturity and affordability continue to lag behind its ambitions.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Two very different research traditions address how people interact with complex data and virtual content: network physicalization, which turns relational or graph data into tangible, manipulable objects, and haptic feedback in AR and VR, which uses actuators to render the sensation of touching a virtual object while the object itself stays purely digital.
The core distinguishing difference is where the interaction lives: physicalization keeps a persistent physical artifact that a person can pick up, rearrange, or walk around without any headset or glove, whereas haptic feedback simulates touch on demand for a virtual scene and requires hardware worn on or against the body to close the loop between vision and touch.
In physicalization projects such as the tangible IP network simulation built by Kobayashi, Hirano, Narita and Ishii, users create new network nodes and modify parameters by placing and moving physical tokens on a table, producing an explorable model of network structure without any digital display of the network itself.
Comparable tangible-token systems, including Urp for urban wind and light simulation, Illuminating Light for optics, and a Micro Smart Grid explainer built on an interactive tabletop, show that mapping relationships onto physical, movable tokens is a recurring design pattern for network and flow data.

Because physicalization keeps a real object in front of the user, it supports exploratory, hands-on learning, since tangible tokens let learners discover a system's underlying structure through direct practical exploration rather than passively reading a diagram.
Physical network representations also support simultaneous multi-user interaction around a shared tabletop, since several people can grab different tokens from different sides of the table at once, an affordance the Micro Smart Grid exhibit relied on for group discussion of energy infrastructure.
Data physicalization research more broadly argues that physical formats can broaden participation, support analytics, and promote creative expression in ways screens cannot, while research on human-data interaction reports that physicalizing sensor and AI data can make it accessible to non-expert audiences.
The rise of low-cost 3D printing and laser cutting has made physicalization more resourceful for researchers, since digital-physical toolkits let designers rapidly prototype tangible network models from inexpensive, reusable materials rather than commissioning custom electronics.

Physicalization remains a comparatively niche and early-stage research area, with visualization researchers and interdisciplinary seminar participants both describing it as historically marginal, with open conceptual, technical, and empirical questions still unresolved.
Because physical tokens are, in Ishii and Ullmer's phrase, relatively inflexible compared with digital bits, once a network model is fabricated it is hard to reconfigure for a different dataset, and the Micro Smart Grid team found that even adding reflective plastic to tokens created new material trade-offs.
Fabrication itself creates accessibility barriers for common users, since small, low-cost actuators for shape-changing displays are still limited in resolution and availability, and toolkit studies found lay designers struggling with assembly instructions, material choice, and precise alignment.
Physical setups can also be environmentally fragile, since the infrared-tracked tangible tabletop in the Micro Smart Grid case required constant readjustment under changing ambient light and heat and was vulnerable to the physical wear of exhibition handling.

Haptic feedback in AR and VR benefits from a well-funded, rapidly growing industry, with the global haptic technology market valued at 8.08 billion US dollars in 2022 and a projected 6.2 percent annual growth rate spanning consumer electronics, automotive, gaming, and healthcare.
Large industrial labs such as Meta's Reality Labs Research have invested years of multidisciplinary work in soft robotics, microfluidics, hand tracking, and perceptual science specifically to make haptic gloves feel believable, illustrating substantial institutional resourcefulness behind the approach.
Haptic feedback generalizes across many use cases without needing a bespoke physical build for every dataset, since wearable haptic devices have been validated for exploring texture, stiffness, size, shape, temperature, weight, and orientation, and tele-haptics extend the same sensors to remote human-to-human interaction.
